steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing DyVal, a dynamic evaluation protocol for LLMs that generates reasoning test samples on the fly with controllable complexity. Cover why LLM evaluation matters, existing benchmarks and their problems, our method, the experiments we ran, key findings and contributions.

steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently reached unprecedented performance on many diverse tasks. This great endeavor has led to positive speculation that LLMs could be precursors of artificial general intelligence, and this means we need to create nuanced evaluations. Evaluation pinpoints the gaps for improvement, so it is the bedrock that improves our understanding of current models and makes sure that AI keeps progressing.

Efforts to evaluate LLMs have intensified a lot. Prior work introduced HELM, which gives a holistic assessment of LLMs in various scenarios. Chatbot Arena is similar and evaluates LLMs by contrasting the output they generate. Other benchmarks which have set the standard for LLM evaluation are AlpacaEval, C-Eval, ARB, API-Bank, Socket, and Big-Bench. Manual experiments have also appeared as a complement to these benchmarks, with works such as one study and another one. Besides these, human evaluators have also been instrumental for gauging what LLMs can do, as discussed by some works and others.

Current evaluation benchmarks have two fundamental challenges. The first is data contamination. A lot of benchmarks take their data from the Internet, so there can be overlap with the huge corpus the LLMs are trained on, and this leads to the debate of “Generalization vs. Memorization”: do the results of the model come from genuine ability or just from memorizing the training data? A recent example is given by one study: LLMs can ambiguously deduce the conclusion that altitude influences temperature from seen data. Similarly, another study found that LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to infer “B is A”, which raises doubt that the abilities of LLMs might come from memorization. The second challenge is static datasets and fixed complexity. LLMs progress very fast, and existing datasets usually fail to match their ever-evolving capabilities, because the complexity level of existing benchmarks is usually static and fixed. As prior work demonstrated, LLMs handle simple problems pretty well but fail on complex problems. Static benchmarks can't increase complexity levels automatically and dynamically based on existing data, and this prevents them from being adapted to accurately select, compare, and advance LLMs. There are a few existing dynamic benchmarks, like DynaBench and DynaBoard, but they depend on crowd-sourcing for data collection, which can be expensive and tedious.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently reached unprecedented performance on many diverse tasks. This great endeavor has led to positive speculation that LLMs could be precursors of artificial general intelligence, and this means we need to create nuanced evaluations. Evaluation pinpoints the gaps for improvement, so it is the bedrock that improves our understanding of current models and makes sure that AI keeps progressing.

Efforts to evaluate LLMs have intensified a lot. Prior work introduced HELM, which gives a holistic assessment of LLMs in various scenarios. Chatbot Arena is similar and evaluates LLMs by contrasting the output they generate. Other benchmarks which have set the standard for LLM evaluation are AlpacaEval, C-Eval, ARB, API-Bank, Socket, and Big-Bench. Manual experiments have also appeared as a complement to these benchmarks, with works such as one study and another one. Besides these, human evaluators have also been instrumental for gauging what LLMs can do, as discussed by some works and others.

Current evaluation benchmarks have two fundamental challenges. The first is data contamination. A lot of benchmarks take their data from the Internet, so there can be overlap with the huge corpus the LLMs are trained on, and this leads to the debate of “Generalization vs. Memorization”: do the results of the model come from genuine ability or just from memorizing the training data? A recent example is given by one study: LLMs can ambiguously deduce the conclusion that altitude influences temperature from seen data. Similarly, another study found that LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to infer “B is A”, which raises doubt that the abilities of LLMs might come from memorization. The second challenge is static datasets and fixed complexity. LLMs progress very fast, and existing datasets usually fail to match their ever-evolving capabilities, because the complexity level of existing benchmarks is usually static and fixed. As prior work demonstrated, LLMs handle simple problems pretty well but fail on complex problems. Static benchmarks can't increase complexity levels automatically and dynamically based on existing data, and this prevents them from being adapted to accurately select, compare, and advance LLMs. There are a few existing dynamic benchmarks, like DynaBench and DynaBoard, but they depend on crowd-sourcing for data collection, which can be expensive and tedious.

In this paper we introduce DyVal, which is a novel, general, and flexible evaluation protocol for dynamic evaluation of LLMs (Sec. 3.1). The core idea of DyVal is to generate evaluation samples dynamically on the fly, instead of collecting a fixed set of data. DyVal has three components: 1) the generation algorithm \mathcal{G} which generates test samples with diversities; 2) the constraint \mathcal{C} which modulates sample complexity and validity; and 3) the description function \mathcal{F} which translates the generated samples into natural languages. Based on this framework we propose a graph-informed DyVal (Sec. 3.2, Figure 1) that generates data using graphs. We are inspired by techniques like the compiler principle and parsing trees which decompose complexities, and we use directed acyclic graphs (DAG) to compose fundamental elements into more intricate problems, where each unit is a graph node. Graph generation is extendable and stochastic, so it regulates complexity levels effectively. Graphs are also hierarchical, which makes them suitable for multi-step inferential tasks like logics. The problems generated by DyVal need a profound understanding of problem solving and not simple memorization, and they also echo how humans solve problems incrementally and derive solutions. Since it is general and flexible, DyVal co-exists and co-evolves with existing benchmarks for better LLMs evaluation and evolution.

We use DyVal to synthesize 7 reasoning tasks: (1) Mathematics: arithmetic and linear equations; (2) Logical reasoning: boolean, deductive, and abductive logic; (3) Algorithm: reachability and maximum sum path problems. Then we re-examine state-of-the-art LLMs with DyVal, from Flan-T5-large, phi-1.5, Xwin-13B, Llama2-13B-chat, Vicuna-13B-v1.3, WizardMath-13B, to GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4. We also test recent prompting techniques, including Few-shot, CoT, Least to Most prompting, Automatic Prompt Engineering, and Skills-in-Context prompting. Finally, we do a human study with 82 human evaluators for comparison, and fine-tuning experiments using evaluation samples generated by DyVal. Experiments on existing benchmarks also show that fine-tuning LLMs on DyVal data can directly improve the abilities of the models without extra careful collection of training data. We also show that DyVal is flexible by extending it to natural language tasks in Appendix H. Our key findings are:

- • Results on DyVal are not always consistent with the results on existing benchmarks, which indicates possible low training data quality and/or data contamination of existing LLMs (Sec. 4.2). For example, phi-1.5, WizardMath-13B, and Xwin-13B do poorly on DyVal even though they claim huge improvements on existing benchmarks.

- • When difficulty increases, LLMs tend to do worse and the gap in their performance becomes larger, which emphasizes that current LLMs lack compositionality and that evaluations with evolving complexity are important (Sec. 4.2).

- • Our error analysis on DyVal shows various failure patterns, which shed light on how LLMs can be improved further. (Sec. 4.3).

- • No prompt engineering method performs best in all our evaluation sets; and larger models tend to do better (Sec. 4.4).

- • DyVal can also be used to generate training data that improves the abilities of LLMs. (Sec. 5). For example, fine-tuning the Llama2 models on data generated by DyVal gives better results on 6 existing benchmarks.

To sum up, the contributions of this paper are:

- • A dynamic evaluation protocol. DyVal is a dynamic evaluation protocol which generates test samples dynamically, and this mitigates the problems of data contamination and static complexity.

- • A graph-informed DyVal algorithm to evaluate the reasoning abilities of LLMs. We use DAGs to compose 7 reasoning problems, from mathematics and logical reasoning to algorithms.

- • Extensive experiments and analysis. We do extensive experiments that give insights for evaluating and improving LLMs.

steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently achieved unprecedented performance across diverse tasks [1,2]. This great endeavor has led to positive speculation on the possibility of LLMs being precursors of artificial general intelligence, which necessitates the creation of nuanced evaluations. By pinpointing gaps for improvement, evaluation becomes the bedrock that enhances the understanding of current models and ensures AI’s continued progression.

Efforts to evaluate LLMs have intensified significantly. [3] introduced HELM, which offers a holistic assessment of LLMs in various scenarios. Similarly, Chatbot Arena [4] evaluates LLMs by contrasting their generated output. Other benchmarks that have set the standard for LLM evaluation include AlpacaEval [5], C-Eval [6], ARB [7], API-Bank [8], Socket [9], and Big-Bench [10]. Moreover, manual experiments have emerged as a complementary approach to these benchmarks, with works such as [2] and [11]. Complementing these, human evaluators have also been instrumental in gauging the prowess of LLMs, as discussed by [12] and [13].

Current evaluation benchmarks face two fundamental challenges. First, data contamination. Many benchmarks source their data from the Internet, causing potential overlap with the vast corpus on which LLMs are trained and leading to the debate of “Generalization vs. Memorization” [14,15,16,17]: are the model’s results stemming from genuine ability or just memorization of the training data? A recent example is provided by [13]: LLMs can ambiguously deduce the conclusion that altitude influences temperature based on seen data. Similarly, [18] found that LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to infer “B is A”, which raises doubts that the abilities of LLMs might come from memorization. Second, static datasets and fixed complexity. As LLMs progress at a rapid pace, existing datasets usually fail to match the models’ ever-evolving capabilities, because the complexity level of existing benchmarks is usually static and fixed. As [19] demonstrated, while handling simple problems pretty well, LLMs fail to solve complex problems. The inability to automatically and dynamically increase complexity levels based on existing data prevents static benchmarks from being adapted to accurately select, compare, and advance LLMs. Although there are a few existing dynamic benchmarks like DynaBench [20] and DynaBoard [21], they rely on crowd-sourcing for data collection, which might be expensive and tedious.

In this paper, we introduce DyVal, a novel, general, and flexible evaluation protocol for the dynamic evaluation of LLMs (Sec. 3.1). The core of DyVal is to dynamically generate evaluation samples on the fly instead of collecting a fixed set of data. DyVal consists of three components: 1) the generation algorithm \mathcal{G} to generate test samples with diversities; 2) the constraint \mathcal{C} to modulate sample complexity and validity; and 3) the description function \mathcal{F} to translate the generated samples into natural languages. Based on this framework, we propose a graph-informed DyVal (Sec. 3.2, Figure 1) that generates data using graphs. Specifically, inspired by techniques such as the compiler principle [22] and parsing trees which decompose complexities [23,24], we employ directed acyclic graphs (DAG) [25] to compose fundamental elements into more intricate problems, with each unit symbolized as a graph node. The extendable and stochastic nature of graph generation effectively regulates the complexity levels. In addition, the hierarchical attributes of graphs make them suitable for multi-step inferential tasks like logics. Problems generated by DyVal require a profound understanding of problem solving rather than simple memorization, and also echo the human approach to incremental problem-solving and solution derivation. Being general and flexible, DyVal co-exists and co-evolves with existing benchmarks for better LLMs evaluation and evolution.

We leverage DyVal to synthesize 7 reasoning tasks, encompassing: (1) Mathematics: arithmetic and linear equations; (2) Logical reasoning: boolean, deductive, and abductive logic; (3) Algorithm: reachability and maximum sum path problems. We then re-examine state-of-the-art LLMs with DyVal, ranging from Flan-T5-large [26], phi-1.5 [27], Xwin-13B [28], Llama2-13B-chat [29], Vicuna-13B-v1.3 [30], WizardMath-13B [31], to GPT-3.5-Turbo [32] and GPT-4 [1]. We also test recent prompting techniques including Few-shot [33], CoT [34], Least to Most prompting [35], Automatic Prompt Engineering [36], and Skills-in-Context prompting [37]. Finally, we perform a human study involving 82 human evaluators for comparison, as well as fine-tuning experiments using DyVal-generated evaluation samples. Experiments on existing benchmarks also show that fine-tuning LLMs with data generated by DyVal can directly improve the models’ abilities without extra careful collection of training data [38]. We further show the flexibility of DyVal by extending it to natural language tasks in Appendix H. Our key findings are:

- • Results on DyVal evaluation are not always consistent with those on existing benchmarks, indicating possible low training data quality and/or data contamination of existing LLMs (Sec. 4.2). For instance, phi-1.5, WizardMath-13B, and Xwin-13B perform poorly on DyVal while claiming huge improvements on existing benchmarks.

- • As difficulty increases, LLMs tend to perform worse and their performance gap becomes larger, emphasizing the lack of compositionality of current LLMs and the importance of evaluations with evolving complexity (Sec. 4.2).

- • Our error analysis based on DyVal evaluation exhibits various failure patterns which shed light on how to further improve LLMs. (Sec. 4.3).

- • No prompt engineering method performs best in all of our evaluation sets; and larger models tend to achieve better performance (Sec. 4.4).

- • DyVal can further be utilized to generate training data that improves the abilities of LLMs. (Sec. 5). For instance, fine-tuning the Llama2 models with DyVal-generated data shows enhanced results on 6 existing benchmarks.

To sum up, this paper makes the following contributions:

- • A dynamic evaluation protocol. DyVal is a dynamic evaluation protocol designed to generate test samples dynamically, mitigating the issues of data contamination and static complexity.

- • A graph-informed DyVal algorithm for evaluating the reasoning abilities of LLMs. We use DAGs to compose 7 reasoning problems from mathematics, logical reasoning to algorithms.

- • Extensive experiments and analysis. We conduct extensive experiments that provide insights for evaluating and improving LLMs.
